#5664. Lost in the Labyrinth of Nicotine Products

— Clinicians need a better way to talk about nicotine risk

Americans increasingly navigate a fast-changing marketplace of nicotine and tobacco products. Walk into a convenience store today and you will encounter a dizzying array of products: cigarettes, e-cigarettes, nicotine pouches, smokeless tobacco, snus, and heated tobacco products, often sold in bright packaging and flavors designed to appeal.

Accompanying this is a confusing information environment. Public health campaigns warn about the dangers of using any tobacco, while the FDA has authorized certain products to carry a modified-risk claim. News stories describe an epidemic of youth vaping, while research reports find that e-cigarettes can help adult smokers quit. Marketing of nicotine and tobacco products often features young, healthy-looking individuals engaged in athletic activities and promises "smoke-free" or "cleaner" experiences, while warnings on products emphasize the dangers of use.

A recent op-ed asserting that the risk of nicotine and tobacco products operates on a continuum illustrates the confusion. Although the byline was attributed to Tom Price, MD, former HHS secretary, a disclosure at the end of the article indicates that it was, in fact, produced in partnership with and paid for by PMI Corporate Services Inc. (Philip Morris International -- a major tobacco company).

While no tobacco products are completely safe, the FDA has recognized that combustible tobacco products (i.e., products that are burned and smoked) like cigarettes pose the greatest health risks and that noncombustible products generally fall lower on the risk spectrum. Reflecting this, the agency has permitted certain products to be marketed with a modified-risk claim that using those products instead of cigarettes reduces the risk of several serious diseases.

As researchers in tobacco communication and regulatory science, we argue that public health agencies and healthcare practitioners have a responsibility to help people navigate this complicated environment. As the nicotine and tobacco marketplace changes, so should our communication about the harm of these products. Individuals in the U.S. are confronted with an assortment of seemingly conflicting messages about nicotine and tobacco products. It is easy to see why people might not fully understand that different products present varying harms.

For someone who does not use any nicotine or tobacco products, the advice is straightforward: Don't start. Nicotine is addictive, and products containing nicotine present a variety of risks, including cardiovascular diseases. For someone who smokes cigarettes, quitting entirely is the best option, and approved treatments such as nicotine patches, gum, and lozenges, and prescription medications should generally be considered as first-line approaches.

But real life is rarely so tidy. Some people try repeatedly to quit and cannot. Others are not yet ready to give up using nicotine and tobacco products. For them, understanding the differences in risk between continuing to smoke cigarettes and using nicotine and tobacco products that are not burnt can impact their health. Eliminating cigarette smoke exposure, even if someone continues to use nicotine and tobacco, can lead to a meaningful reduction in harm.

Clinicians have recommended considering e-cigarettes as a smoking cessation tool for patients who smoke. However, as the marketplace expands far beyond e-cigarettes, doctors, public health agencies, and other trusted voices should be prepared to explain a continuum of risk among various nicotine and tobacco products rather than centering on any single product. This does not mean handing smokers a shopping list. It does not mean calling vapes, nicotine pouches, or smokeless tobacco harmless. And it certainly does not mean encouraging people who do not currently use nicotine to start.

It means being transparent about what we know: Cigarettes are extraordinarily dangerous, and nicotine is what makes them so hard to quit. Some other products can deliver nicotine, but carry substantially lower risks to one's health. Switching completely matters, and using cigarettes alongside another product does not deliver the same risk reduction.

To be clear, we do not know for certain the best way to deliver the information to people who smoke. It could be conversations between healthcare providers and their patients, public education campaigns, a trusted source anyone can consult easily, or some combination of the above. Each approach has trade-offs in reach, cost, and the risk of unintended consequences. What we need is evidence on which approaches help smokers understand relative risk without encouraging nicotine and tobacco product use among people who otherwise would not start.

One key principle is ensuring that whatever the format this communication takes, the information comes from credible and independent sources with no stake in selling these products.

This conversation cannot wait because people are already hearing claims in ads and on social media about reduced harm of certain nicotine and tobacco products. Influencers portray nicotine pouches as a lifestyle, with talk of "upper deckies" and what it means to be a "Zynner." Increasingly, people will see modified-risk claims that the FDA has authorized. If health professionals respond with silence or oversimplified messages, the tobacco industry, social media, and word of mouth will fill the gap. Communication revolving around nicotine and tobacco product harm should help people make sense of the growing array of products and understand how each one works and what risks they carry.

Some worry that acknowledging reduced-risk products sounds like endorsing the tobacco industry. Given the industry's history of deceiving consumers about the risks presented by tobacco, skepticism is warranted. But withholding meaningful information, supported by evidence from the scientific community, on the risk differences is not the answer.

We can hold two ideas at once: No nicotine or tobacco product is safe, and some products are far more dangerous than others. For decades, public health has taught Americans how dangerous cigarettes are, and we should not undermine that achievement. But an evolving marketplace demands an evolving message -- one that tells people not only what to avoid, but how products differ, what switching can and cannot accomplish, and where the evidence remains uncertain. Americans navigating an increasingly complicated nicotine marketplace deserve an accurate roadmap to protect the public's health.

The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the NIH.

#5663. Mayo Clinic Platform launches AI-driven clinical decision support tool

Mayo Clinic Platform launches AI-driven clinical decision support tool" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Mayo Clinic launched an AI-enabled clinical decision support solution embedded directly in electronic health record workflows. The CDS solution will put Mayo’s clinical knowledge and evidence-informed guidance at the point of care, rather than requiring clinicians to search across separate resources.

Mayo Clinic Platform, a strategic initiative from the Rochester, Minn.-based health system, developed the tool, and it will be expanded and updated over time, executives said. The solution draws on multiple clinical tools, reducing the need for clinicians to navigate independent resources to find trusted clinical information.

Mayo Clinic is making the CDS tool available to Mayo Clinic clinicians as well as healthcare organizations participating in Mayo Clinic Platform's provider programs. Mayo Clinic is essentially turning its clinical expertise into scalable AI infrastructure available beyond its own health system.

Beginning in November, eligible clinicians will have access to two key capabilities: a specialty-specific chat that covers more than 35 specialties and 22 clinical calculators available via chat or voice dictation.

Powered by a large language model, the specialty-specific AI chat tool surfaces relevant information to help clinicians reason through complex cases and cites responses from peer-reviewed literature. The tool is updated daily, giving clinicians access to relevant emerging evidence alongside established medical knowledge, executives said. The tool helps clinicians quickly answer patient-specific clinical questions, explore differential diagnoses and evaluate care options. And the specialty-specific AI chat mirrors Mayo Clinic's subspecialty model of care.

The clinical calculators, spanning cardiology, oncology, hepatology, endocrinology and other specialty use cases, provide industry-standard medical information and evidence-based decision support on clinical questions and patient care context. Proprietary Mayo Clinic-developed calculators are included in this tool, according to the health system.

"Clinicians have access to a vast amount of medical knowledge, but finding relevant information for individualized patient care takes valuable time," said Maneesh Goyal, Mayo Clinic Platform chief operating officer, in a statement. "With this new solution, we are bringing trusted Mayo Clinic knowledge directly into the clinical workflow so clinicians can spend less time searching for information across multiple resources and more time focused on patient care."

The platform is "designed to evolve" as new tools are added to Mayo Clinic Platform, executives say.

David C. and Flora C. Pratt Distinguished Chief Medical Officer for Mayo Clinic Platform Gelareh Zadeh, M.D., Ph.D., said in a statement the solution "does not replace clinical judgment."

"Mayo Clinic physicians have provided feedback on the different tools to ensure the solution supports clinicians and reflects Mayo Clinic's approach to patient care," Zadeh said.

#5662. Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken

Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in almost the opposite way of previously known defenses. The surprising mechanism allows bacteria to activate a deadly self-destruct process when viruses attack, potentially offering new ideas for developing medical treatments and gene-editing technologies.

The findings, published in Molecular Cell, reveal how a group of bacterial defense systems called "type VI retrons" use an unexpectedly complex sequence of molecular events to fight infection. Unlike other retrons, these systems rely on DNA to activate a toxin rather than keep one suppressed.

Understanding this unusual process could do more than expand scientists' knowledge of bacterial immunity. It may also provide a foundation for designing more effective DNA-editing tools, potentially allowing researchers to correct harmful genetic mutations with greater precision.

"This is, by far, the strangest of the retron systems that we or anyone else has come across," says Gladstone Investigator Seth Shipman, PhD, senior author of the new study. "These retrons operate with Rube Goldberg-level complexity, using molecular mechanisms that we would never have thought to invent, but that we'll use in future technologies."

How Bacteria Sacrifice Themselves to Stop Viruses

Bacteria face constant threats from viruses known as phages, which infect bacterial cells and use their machinery to reproduce. Over time, bacteria have evolved a variety of defenses to prevent these viruses from spreading.

Among these defenses are retrons, molecular systems that can detect certain viral infections and trigger the infected bacterium to destroy itself. Although this sacrifice kills the individual cell, it prevents the virus from producing more copies and infecting nearby bacteria, helping protect the larger colony.

Retrons are also of considerable interest to scientists developing new genetic technologies. They can efficiently produce and deliver single-stranded DNA, making them promising tools for editing DNA inside human cells. Shipman's team and other researchers are investigating whether these capabilities could eventually be used to correct mutations responsible for disease with exceptional accuracy.

Until now, scientists believed they understood the basic way retron defenses operate.

In previously studied retrons, a toxic protein is already present inside an uninfected cell, but its harmful effects are held in check by short pieces of single-stranded DNA. When a phage infects the bacterium, it disrupts this protective arrangement, allowing the toxin to act. The resulting cell death prevents the virus from spreading.

The newly investigated type VI retrons, however, did not appear to follow this familiar pattern.

A Bacterial Immune System That Works Backward

Researchers first became suspicious that type VI retrons were different when they could not detect the single-stranded DNA normally associated with these systems.

"The way we typically detect retrons inside uninfected cells is by looking for this single-stranded DNA," says Karen Zhang, a PhD student in Shipman's lab and lead author of the study. "But type VI retrons caught our attention because they didn't appear to have this signature. It was very odd, and we wondered if they might be broken."

Despite their unusual behavior, experiments showed that bacteria carrying type VI retrons could still defend themselves against phage infections. The systems were clearly functional, even though they lacked the expected molecular signs of activity.

"That kicked off a long molecular odyssey," Shipman says. "Whenever we tried the experiments we normally use to study retrons, they would fail, so we kept having to think of new ways to figure out how these retrons work."

After extensive investigation, the team discovered that type VI retrons reverse a key step in the usual defense process.

Rather than maintaining a substantial supply of single-stranded DNA and toxin before infection, these retrons produce little detectable DNA and no noticeable amount of toxin in healthy cells. The arrival of a phage triggers a sharp increase in DNA production.

As the DNA accumulates, it interacts with an RNA molecule that has been preventing the toxin from being made. This interaction removes the restriction, allowing the bacterium to rapidly produce the toxic protein.

The toxin appears to be an exceptionally small protein that inserts itself into the bacterium's surrounding cell membrane. By disrupting the membrane's stability, it causes the infected cell to die, stopping the viral infection from spreading.

In other words, the DNA acts as an activation switch rather than a restraint. Instead of preventing an existing toxin from causing harm, it helps turn on toxin production only when the bacterium detects a threat.

"It's almost the mirror-image version of how we traditionally view retrons, because the DNA switches on toxin production instead of inhibiting an already-produced toxin," Zhang says. "It would be fascinating to explore how bacterial evolution could have resulted in such a complex molecular system -- whether type VI retrons are older or newer than other retrons, or whether they're a stepping stone between different types."

An Unusual Discovery Required New Experiments

Figuring out how type VI retrons function proved unusually difficult. Many established techniques that scientists use to examine retrons repeatedly produced no useful results, forcing the team to develop new experimental strategies and adapt existing methods.

One particularly important challenge involved detecting the DNA produced by type VI retrons in cells that had not been infected.

After conventional tests failed, the researchers tried a technique called Spacer-seq, which had previously been developed in Shipman's laboratory. The method uses components of CRISPR-Cas, another bacterial immune system, to record molecular activity inside cells.

CRISPR-Cas is best known for its role in modern gene-editing technologies, but bacteria originally evolved these systems as defenses against viruses. Spacer-seq takes advantage of this natural machinery to help researchers investigate what happens inside cells.

The alternative approach finally revealed a trace amount of single-stranded DNA that earlier experiments had missed.

"We had just about given up hope that any DNA was being made when this approach finally revealed a very, very low level of production in uninfected cells," Zhang says.

This breakthrough encouraged the researchers to continue investigating. Additional experiments confirmed that type VI retrons produce DNA at very low levels under normal conditions and substantially increase production only after a phage enters the cell.

The findings explained why the defense system had appeared inactive in earlier tests and revealed the unusual sequence of events responsible for its antiviral activity.

Could This Strange Bacterial Defense Lead to New Medical Treatments?

The discovery is already influencing research in Shipman's laboratory, where scientists are exploring ways to transform the type VI retron's natural machinery into useful technologies.

One promising application involves developing synthetic molecular sensors and switches that can regulate gene activity. Such systems could potentially allow researchers to control when particular genes are activated or suppressed, opening new possibilities for studying disease and designing treatments.

"This system represents a unique way to potentially build a molecular sensor and switch encoded in DNA and RNA, that no one has thought of before," Zhang says. "Synthetic sensors and switches have many possible applications, both in treating disease and in designing experiments to better understand how certain diseases operate."

Another possibility involves the retron's unusually small but powerful toxins. Because these proteins can disrupt bacterial membranes and kill cells, researchers are investigating whether they could be adapted into new antimicrobial treatments.

Such therapies could potentially target harmful bacteria responsible for human infections, providing a new approach to combating bacterial disease.

These medical applications remain under development, but the discovery offers researchers a molecular design that would have been difficult to imagine without studying nature's existing solutions.

"This study highlights why it's so important for a molecular technology development lab like ours to keep looking to nature for inspiration," Shipman says. "We can use what evolution has given us as starting points to build complex machines that would have been tremendously hard to even conceptualize."

The research also raises intriguing questions about bacterial evolution, including how such an elaborate defense arose and whether type VI retrons represent an earlier, later, or intermediate stage in the evolution of these immune systems.

For scientists seeking new ways to manipulate DNA, control genes, and fight infections, this backward-acting bacterial defense could provide an unexpected starting point.

The research, "Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein," was published in Molecular Cell on October 13, 2026.

Along with Shipman and Zhang, the authors include Matías Rojas-Montero, Darshini Poola, and Alejandro González-Delgado of Gladstone; Josepha Klas, Arturo Carabias, Dennis Zhang, Mario Mestre, Ruiliang Zhao, Ana Dávila-Hidalgo, Guillermo Montoya, and Rafael Pinilla-Redondo of the University of Copenhagen; and Lieza Chan and Kliment Verba of UC San Francisco.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation, the Robert J. Kleeberg Jr. and Helen C. Kleberg Foundation, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, the Lundbeck Foundation, the Fulbright U.S. Student Program, the Junta de Castilla y León and European Social Fund Plus, the European Molecular Biology Organization, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the European Research Council, and the Villum Foundation.

#5659. Healthcare Dealmakers—Chicago's $11B hospital merger, another health system ASC deal and more

Healthcare Dealmakers—Chicago's $11B hospital merger, another health system ASC deal and more" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare mergers and acquisitions are in no short supply as providers, health tech companies, payers and other industry players look to expand their businesses and gain a competitive edge. Here’s a roundup of new deals that were revealed, closed, rumored or called off during the month of October.

Rush University System for Health and Endeavor Health announced plans to merge, becoming a 12-hospital nonprofit with nearly $11 billion in annual revenue. The resulting entity would command over 400 care sites, employ more than 46,000 people including over 3,400 clinicians, and reach over 2 million Northern Illinois and Northwest Indiana patients per year. The pair are targeting an early 2027 close and outlined plans to commit $1 billion of Endeavor funds toward care in the region.

Private equity firm CD&R and healthcare conglomerate McKesson plan to acquire Option Care Health, a provider of infusion therapy services, in a deal valued at $5.8 billion. The purchase gives equity holders a per-share offer of $32.05 and is expected to close in the first half of 2027. CD&R would be the majority stakeholder in the company, which is the country’s largest independent at-home and alternate site infusion services provider.

Bon Secours Mercy Health announced plans to acquire a majority stake in Surgery Partners, among the country’s largest outpatient surgical care companies, in a take-private deal valuing the acquiree at $5.7 billion. Bain Capital Private Equity will roll over its 39% share of the company as it's purchased by a Bon Secours affiliate at $23.50 per share. Surgery Partners includes more than 200 locations and about 5,000 affiliated physicians across 30 states. The organizations are targeting an early 2027 close.

Risant Health, Kaiser Permanente’s subsidiary value-based care platform, announced Integris Health as its next regional health system acquisition. Financial terms were not disclosed, though the deal aims for an early 2027 close. Integris is Oklahoma’s largest nonprofit provider with 10 acute and 10 specialty hospitals with $3.3 billion in total operating revenues during the 2025 fiscal year.

MultiCare Health System picked up the final needed regulatory approval to absorb Samaritan Health Services during October. The nonprofits then consummated their 18-hospital combination on Nov. 1.

Hackensack Meridian Health has signed a definitive agreement to pick up Central New Jersey’s Hunterdon Health, which would grow the state’s largest health system to 19 total hospitals. The agreement outlines a $200 million capital investment from Hackensack Meridian, plus another $30 million to roll out Epic’s electronic health record.

Cencora (formerly AmerisourceBergen) signed a definitive agreement to acquire American Oncology Network, a collection of more than 350 oncology providers, in a deal valuing the network at $2.4 billion. Cencora said it expects to pay $1.7 billion to increase its 4% interest to 75%.

Parkview Health is acquiring Ovation Healthcare, a nationwide shared services vendor for providers. The 16-hospital Indiana nonprofit did not disclose financial terms, but said it hopes to close the deal within weeks. Parkview views the pickup as an opportunity to boost its administrative capabilities, which could be offered to other rural systems.

Parkview Health also wrapped its acquisition of Goshen Health, a 105-bed hospital with a network of physicians.

Independence Health System, a five-hospital nonprofit in western Pennsylvania, joined the West Virginia University Health System on Oct. 1. The deal was announced late last year and brings a five-year, $800 million capital commitment from WVU Health System toward the Independence hospitals and communities, which will "immediately" begin operating under the WVU Medicine brand.

Kettering Health plans to add Knox Community Hospital as its 15th medical center. The Ohio systems signed a definitive agreement for their deal, which will include undisclosed commitments toward Knox’s facilities, equipment and technology.

Nationwide Children’s Hospital plans to acquire the pediatric practice of Knox Community Hospital in spring 2027. Nationwide plans to combine the practice with one of its affiliates and continue providing services to Knox.

Allegiance Health Management said it plans to divest four Louisiana hospitals: Minden Medical Center, Northern Louisiana Medical Center, Acadian Medical Center and Mercy Regional Medical Center. No potential buyers or deal timelines were given.

Orlando Health closed its acquisition of RMC Health System, an Alabama organization with a 375-bed medical center. The deal was first announced in April, and brings five years of “significant” investment into RMC’s facilities, equipment and technology.

HCA Healthcare sold 31 home health and hospital agencies to Deaconess Associations. The facilities were located across eight states. Financial terms were not disclosed.

MaineHealth added York Hospital to its Southern region, marking the 79-bed facility as the system’s tenth hospital.

Ascension Seton said it is acquiring three locations in the greater Austin area from Family Health Systems, one of which is the Auton-based Family Hospital. The deal is set to close later this year.

Cone Health entered an agreement to acquire three pharmacies in Reidsville, North Carolina: Carolina Apothecary, Belmont Pharmacy and Rx Care.

Humana struck a deal shifting out Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe for BlackRock for equity in a joint venture running about 150 of its CenterWell locations. The deal sees BlackRock buying out WCAS’ equity for about $2.8 billion.

Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield of New Jersey is acquiring the New Jersey operations of Summit Health, which includes CityMD urgent care sites. Financial details or a potential timeline were not disclosed.

Redesign Health plans to merge with Sheba Medical Center’s innovation arm, ARC Global, creating a roughly $2 billion company. The pair hope to build an end-to-end platform that helps health systems to turn ideas originating with their own clinicians and operators into technology products and standalone companies that can then be scaled across a global network. To help do so, the pair also agreed to acquire strategic advisory and intelligence firm AVIA.

Teladoc Health acquired Teledigm Health, which provides hybrid clinical services and specialized care support for rural and regional health systems, the public virtual care company announced alongside its Q3 earnings. Financial terms were not disclosed. Teladoc leadership said picking up its longtime partner will help it grow with providers serving rural communities.

RadNet, an imaging center operator and seller of radiology technology, is acquiring Onrad, a teleradiology services company with 130 contracted radiologists. The deal is expected to close early next year and will bring Onrad shareholders a collective $350 million plus 5 million RadNet shares, with additional performance-based earnouts.

iRhythm wrapped its acquisition of cardiac remote patient monitoring company VitalConnect for $237.5 million. The deal will help iRhythm evolve from ambulatory cardiac monitoring toward “a broader cardiac monitoring and intelligence platform,” its CEO and president told Fierce Healthcare.

Zocdoc acquired insurance technology company Sohar Health, the first acquisition in its nearly 20-year history and part of its push to evolve beyond an appointment-booking marketplace into broader healthcare access infrastructure. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Carenet Health, which provides patient engagement and navigation tools to over 400 healthcare partners, acquired Orbita, an AI engagement and communication company that does business with providers. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Tegria, a healthcare consultancy and services company, acquired cybersecurity, cloud hosting and managed IT services company CloudWave for an undisclosed sum.

Chapter, a Medicare navigation and retirement advisory company, has acquired Hively, a personalized retirement navigation and membership startup, for an undisclosed sum. The pair intend to launch in-person and online community programming for retirees surrounding retirement and aging topics, a move beyond Medicare navigation alone.

Sagility, a provider and payer technology services company, acquired Chirok Health, which offers clinical documentation improvement, medical coding and revenue integrity services for an undisclosed sum.

Investment firm Sopris Capital said it acquired Blackford Analysis, an AI medical imaging platform, from Bayer for an undisclosed sum. Sopris said it intends to deploy the company’s tools across its healthcare portfolio.

Emergence, a private equity firm, acquired digital intake and online reputation management software company Clinect for an undisclosed sum.

#5657. Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months

A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.

The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).

The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.

Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous

Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.

Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.

Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.

To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.

The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.

The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.

One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).

The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.

At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.

Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.

During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).

This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).

After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.

More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission

Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).

Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.

The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.

After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.

Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.

Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.

After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.

Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects

No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.

At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.

The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.

The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.

"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."

Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters

One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.

The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.

Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.

Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.

To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.

They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."

A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes

The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.

People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.

The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.

They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.

However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.

The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

Materials provided by European Association for the Study of Diabetes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5656. Adjunctive L-Methylfolate Tied to Executive Function Gains in Psychiatric Patients

— Real-world study found symptom improvements scaled with number of prior meds tried

In treatment-experienced psychiatric patients receiving established pharmacotherapy, adjunctive L-methylfolate (Deplin) was linked with significant reductions in overall symptom burden and improvements in executive function, according to retrospective chart review data.

Among 60 patients, initiation of L-methylfolate was associated with a significant incremental reduction in overall symptom burden, with an average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) of -0.14 SD (95% CI -0.20 to -0.08, P<0.0001), reported Joel Young, MD, of MedaData and the Rochester Center for Behavioral Medicine (RCBM) in Michigan, and colleagues.

This was a pooled outcome assessed using the ADHD Symptom and Side Effect Tracking scale (ASSET), the Patient Health Questionnaire 9-item scale (PHQ-9), and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7).

Each individual outcome measure showed improvement, with the largest effect observed in executive function:

The study was presented at the Neuroscience Education Institute (NEI) Fall Congress in Colorado Springs, Colorado.

"What caught my attention most was the pattern of improvement: patients' executive-function scores showed the largest and earliest change, with depression and anxiety improving more gradually," co-author Richard Powell, PhD, JD, also of MedaData and RCBM, told MedPage Today.

"Seeing that pattern in patients who were already receiving psychiatric treatment was encouraging," Powell added.

Prior clinical research has shown benefits from adjunctive L-methylfolate in patients whose depression responded incompletely to standard antidepressants.

"Our study adds a perspective from everyday psychiatric practice: we followed 60 patients before and during Deplin treatment and examined depression, anxiety, and executive-function scores," Powell said. "That broader picture gives us useful questions to pursue about where patients may experience improvement."

L-methylfolate is the biologically active form of folate (vitamin B9) that directly crosses the blood-brain barrier, bypassing enzymatic conversion steps such as MTHFR. Deplin is a prescription medical food formulated for the dietary management of suboptimal folate levels in patients with depression and schizophrenia, intended for use under medical supervision.

"Despite widespread clinical use, the incremental benefit of adjunctive Deplin when added to standard psychiatric treatment, particularly among treatment-experienced patients, has not been well characterized in routine clinical practice," the authors noted on their poster.

To evaluate routine practice outcomes, the researchers used a within-patient interrupted time-series design spanning 2021 to 2026. Out of 131 identified Deplin-treated charts, 60 patients contributed visits both before and during treatment to form the analysis cohort. The GAD-7 was added to clinical surveys in late 2024, resulting in a smaller sample size (n=28) for the anxiety measure. Demographically, the chart-reviewed cohort was 97.7% white and 1.5% Hispanic/Latino.

Symptom reduction was more pronounced among patients with heavier baseline treatment regimens: each additional pre-Deplin medication class was associated with a 0.118 SD greater improvement (mixed-model moderation, P=0.005).

This finding "raises a useful question about who might benefit most," noted Powell. "Ultimately, we want to understand whether the changes we see in symptom scores translate into meaningful improvements in patients' everyday lives."

Secondary analyses demonstrated significant improvements in vegetative (P=0.006), somatic (P=0.044), and behavioral (P=0.040) dimensions, with no assessed side-effect domains worsening significantly during treatment.

In an exploratory analysis of 23 stimulant-treated patients -- an outcome outside the product's approved dietary management labeling -- dose trajectories shifted from +3.4 to -2.5 mg-eq/year following L-methylfolate initiation (P=0.0004), at a baseline median amphetamine-equivalent dose of 26 mg-eq.

"I'd encourage clinicians to keep asking about persistent symptoms and how patients are managing day to day. L-methylfolate may be an option to consider for appropriate patients with an incomplete response to depression treatment," said Powell.

The study authors highlighted several limitations, emphasizing that regression to the mean remains an alternative explanation in single-arm designs initiated during active symptoms. Because the study was observational and non-randomized, confounding by indication and concurrent regimen adjustments cannot be ruled out. All reported P-values were nominal without multiplicity adjustments.

"Controlled research is needed to clarify how much of the improvement was attributable to L-methylfolate," Powell concluded.

#5654. Omada Health hikes 2026 outlook after ‘strongest quarter ever’ in Q3

Omada Health hikes 2026 outlook after ‘strongest quarter ever’ in Q3" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Omada Health saw its "strongest quarter ever" in the third quarter of 2026, CEO and co-founder Sean Duffy told investors and analysts during a Thursday evening earnings call.

"We delivered our highest quarterly revenue, gross margin progression, and our most profitable quarter to date," Duffy said.

The virtual chronic care provider, which went public last June, brought in $91 million in revenue—up 34% year-over-year—and reported gross margin of 76% on a GAAP basis and 78% on a non-GAAP basis, according to Duffy. Omada reported net income of $7 million in the third quarter, compared with a net loss of $3 million in Q3 2025.

The company also reported adjusted EBITDA of $12 million, compared to $2 million the year prior.

It beat Wall Street analysts’ estimates for revenue, though slightly trailed behind projections for total membership.

Total members reached 1.1 million, up 36% year-over-year, with trailing 12-month revenue per total member increasing 5% year-over-year to $294, according to financial results published Thursday. Average member tenure also grew 10% compared to the year prior, to approximately two years and four months. Member retention has improved to 58%, up from 43% in Q4 of 2024, executives said.

Omada Health President Wei-Li Shao said Q3 membership growth reflects "continued demand" for its cardiometabolic platform, adding that the company's diabetes and hypertension programs continued to lead growth.

The company's diabetes and hypertension programs, longer member retention and lower care delivery costs are increasingly driving both growth and profitability, executives said.

"Members stayed with us longer, and our ability to provide personalized care at scale reached a new level of efficiency," Shao said.

The company supports diabetes, hypertension, obesity and musculoskeletal conditions—launching a GLP-1 care companion solution last November.

Shao noted that Omada deepened its partnership with the Health Care Services Corporation (HCSC) last quarter to extend its prevention and hypertension programs into three additional states, which is expected to "potentially reach an additional estimated 1.5 million covered lives at launch in 2027."

"On the PBM side, we have commercial relationships with the three largest PBMs in the country, which together processed an estimated 80% of prescription claims in 2025," Shao said. "Our prescribing program is in the market now at Optum. These relationships give us the broadest distribution in Omada’s history for our programs."

Shao, who will take over as CEO Jan. 1, also noted that artificial intelligence solutions enable care teams to have more capacity to "apply their clinical expertise" while tailoring care to each member’s needs.

"This quarter shows what we have built at Omada," Shao said. "Our commercial relationships give us broad reach, and our cardiometabolic programs have driven growth. Our program mix has supported longer member tenure, and our cost to serve has decreased."

Chief Financial Officer Steve Cook told investors the company expects new enrollments to "moderate sequentially" in the fourth quarter, which he said is "consistent with historic seasonality."

Shao also noted that a number of employers have been spending more time making GLP-1 coverage and obesity care decisions, "given the size of the commitment, the range of solutions and the importance of getting these decisions right," which has extended the selling season deeper into the fourth quarter.

Omada Health's stock dropped 19% Friday following the Q3 earnings call on Thursday as investors pulled back due to concerns about the longer selling season and expected Q4 member decline clouding the company's 2027 outlook.

The company is raising its full 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA outlook. Cook said revenue is expected to range from $344 million to $346 million, up from its previous range of $334 million to $340 million. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be in the range of $32 million to $34 million, up from $21 million to $27 million.

"Our outlook anticipates Q4 revenue below our Q3 level, reflecting the lower new enrollment and engagement activity we have historically seen during the holidays," Cook said. "We expect revenue to come primarily from continued engagement among existing members."

#5653. Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake."

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

The new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

"Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance."

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

#5652. Two incoming lawmakers plan to defend health equity from Trump administration cuts

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Anil Oza is a general assignment reporter at STAT focused on the NIH and health equity. You can reach him on Signal at aniloza.16.

Amid a sweep of Democratic victories in Tuesday’s midterms, some online commentators jokingly declared “Woke is back.”

There was little congressional pushback over the past two years as the Trump administration terminated hundreds of grants meant to chronicle and remedy medical inequities, shuttered programs intended to diversify the science workforce, and opened investigations into universities and medical schools it accused of discriminating against white and Asian applicants. Will that change now that the Democratic Party has won control of the 120th Congress?

Two newly elected candidates with science credentials told STAT they hope to change that: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former health disparities researcher, and incoming Rep. Jasmine Clark of Georgia, a microbiologist who will be the first Black woman with a STEM Ph.D. in Congress.

Democrats have a long list of priorities, and with President Trump still wielding his veto power, passing bills related to health equity will still be an uphill battle. The White House posted on X Thursday, “FYI: DEI is still dead.” But, the introduction of at least two lawmakers with personal connections to health equity work could offer a counterweight to such policies for the rest of the second Trump administration.

“I know firsthand what DEI initiatives can do for students who are trying to find their way, and they don’t actually quite know all of the options that are available to them,” Clark told STAT in an interview Wednesday. A former professor, she said such programs have opened up opportunities for her students in the sciences.

El-Sayed, interviewed a few days before the election, said, “The war on diversity, equity, and inclusion is about a vision of an America that doesn’t include certain kinds of people. I will always stand for an America where everybody is included and empowered, and I think that’s critical for us as we move to the future.” During his time in academia, he did research on disparities in maternal health and within the Arab American community. He added, “we need to be able to document the ways in which our systems are allowing for and, in some respects, creating the differences in the ability for people to live long, healthy lives. It’s important work, and it should help guide where public policy gaps are and where we need to fill them.”

The second Trump administration has seen unprecedented changes to the scientific ecosystem. Some of the most major have drawn forceful responses from Congress. Proposals to cut the National Institutes of Health’s budget, cap funding for overhead costs at universities, and exert more political control over federal funding have all been rebuked by Congress. With the Democrats taking control of both chambers, further pushback may be coming.

The NIH did not respond to a request for comment.

A number of physicians and scientists who won their races have noted that accountability for health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is high on their list of priorities. Part of that accountability should be understanding which communities and researchers were affected by policies like grant terminations over the past two years, said Jennifer Jones, who directs the Center for Science and Democracy at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “I want to know who was most harmed by this because there’s absolutely a justice and equity issue at play when you clearly attack issues of diversity, equity, and inclusion,” she said.

While equity work is sometimes portrayed as controversial, Philip Alberti, the founding director of the Association of American Medical Colleges Center for Health Justice, said polling he has done has shown broad support for health equity initiatives across ideological groups. “Three-quarters of U.S. adults support the goal of ‘all communities having a fair and just opportunity to be healthy,’ and 65% of adults who have ever heard the term ‘health equity’ support it, too,” he said. “This was true across all subgroups, including across groups defined by self-identified ideology. This is not controversial.”

Clark trained as a microbiologist before taking to politics during the first Trump administration. She said she would seek an assignment on the House oversight committee and has a number of questions she’d like to pose to appointees like Kennedy. For one, she would like to understand why the administration has repeatedly pushed for a controversial hepatitis B vaccine study in Guinea-Bissau. Clark likened that trial to the Tuskegee syphilis experiment, an unethical study conducted by the U.S. Public Health Service and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that withheld treatment for syphilis from nearly 400 African American men from 1932 to 1972.

Another way she has seen the fallout of the administration is that her former lab, which studies HIV transmission, had to pause some of its longitudinal studies in Africa because of restrictions on international collaborations. Even if the lab is able to find more funding, “you basically have to start from scratch, or you just have a big hole in your data. That’s not what we need to be doing if we want to actually do things like end the HIV epidemic,” she said.

She also lamented the process of grants for federal funding being screened for certain terms and phrases to determine if they are related to “DEI.” This process has particularly affected researchers studying health disparities, and has made it difficult for some to apply for new funding. In September, a handful of researchers sued the agency, arguing this process infringed on their first amendment rights.

“Having the ability to write in your research grant that you’re looking at the disproportionate impact without having to dance around those words because any grant that has the word ‘disproportionate,’ or ‘woman,’ or ‘Black,’ or ‘gender,’ or anything like that all of a sudden gets flagged,” she said. “That’s not the environment we should be operating under if we actually want to answer real-life questions. So I look forward to being a part of a Congress that will prioritize moving toward and not immediately dismissing research because they are trying to answer questions about why one group is impacted more than another.”

Anil Oza is a general assignment reporter at STAT focused on the NIH and health equity. You can reach him on Signal at aniloza.16.

#5651. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5650. Equiti acquires Lexi AI to combine AI, human medical interpretation

Equiti acquires Lexi AI to combine AI, human medical interpretation" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Equiti is acquiring Lexi AI to build a hybrid language-access model that combines AI language support with human medical interpreters.

Equiti, which sells medical interpretation services to hospitals and health systems through its Martti business, provides 24/7 access to qualified medical interpreters across more than 250 languages and dialects. Lexi provides multilingual, AI-powered medical interpretation. The acquisition deal merges Lexi's immediate AI language support, covering over 35 languages and dialects, with Martti and its network of qualified medical interpreters to help healthcare organizations expand language access.

The acquisition was announced October 28. Financial details of the deal were not disclosed.

With this acquisition, Equiti is building on Martti’s work pioneering video remote interpretation in healthcare more than two decades ago, according to executives. The use of AI can expand where and when language services can be offered, particularly for everyday interactions that may not currently receive interpretation support, Equiti executives said.

Martti was built alongside healthcare organizations to make qualified interpreters available by video. Lexi, in turn, has been developed with healthcare customers to extend immediate language support into more workflows. The acquisition brings those capabilities together, with human-in-the-loop design, patient safety and patient experience at its center, Equiti executives said.

The company saw an opportunity to combine its services with Lexi's AI expertise rather than build a healthcare AI interpretation product internally, Maureen Huber, Equiti CEO, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Lexi brings specialized expertise in AI, engineering and healthcare product design, along with experience putting that technology into the hands of care teams. That combination takes time to build," Huber said. "For more than 20 years, our work through Martti has been about making qualified human interpretation accessible within healthcare. We understand the service, the clinical environment and what it takes to support healthcare organizations every day. Developing AI and machine learning technology calls for additional, specialized expertise. We wanted people who had already been doing that work with healthcare in mind."

She added, "We spent time evaluating the category and learning from customers. Lexi brought together the people, product and approach we were seeking. Combining their expertise with ours gives us a stronger foundation to expand language access responsibly."

Combining AI and human interpretation makes language support more accessible across the patient journey, helping organizations improve care delivery while making better use of their resources, according to Equiti executives.

Healthcare organizations are increasingly interested in AI interpretation capabilities and are looking for guidance, Huber noted.

"Customers were asking: 'Where could AI help? How do we evaluate it? What is appropriate for our patients?' Healthcare leaders see the same advances in consumer AI that everyone else sees. They also must think about what happens when those tools enter a care environment, sometimes before an organization has decided how they should be used. They want a partner who understands both the possibilities and the responsibilities," she said.

She added, "I would describe that as inquiry and evaluation. There is real curiosity about extending language support to more of the patient experience, particularly before and after a visit. Our job is to help customers identify those opportunities while keeping qualified human interpretation central to care delivery."

Equiti calls this approach Modality Matters, a connected model that allows healthcare organizations to match each encounter with the appropriate modality — immediate, healthcare-purpose-built AI support for approved use cases and qualified medical interpretation where clinical complexity, regulatory requirements, organizational policy or patient preference calls for a human interpreter. With this approach, organizations have the flexibility to shift between modalities as clinical context and communication needs change in real time.

The combined portfolio of Equiti and Lexi's capabilities will extend language access into everyday interactions that often go unsupported, Huber noted.

Equiti is focusing Lexi's AI-powered medical interpretation on routine patient engagement, including before and after care, such as appointment communications, scheduling and nonclinical follow-up logistics.

"We see a significant opportunity for Lexi in that communication before and after care: helping patients exchange messages, arrange appointments and stay connected in their preferred language. Language access must extend beyond the clinical encounter. Think about what happens after a patient leaves the clinic. They receive a message about a follow-up appointment, but they need to ask whether it is at the same location, how to reschedule, or whom to contact. Those may be simple questions for the organization, but the answers determine whether the patient can take the next step," she said.

Qualified human interpreters remain the foundation for care delivery, Huber noted. "In conversations such as those about a diagnosis, informed consent, treatment or palliative care, the ability to clarify meaning, recognize cultural context and respond with empathy is essential. A medically qualified interpreter helps people understand one another through conversations that can be complex and deeply personal," she said.

Equiti said it can work with customers to define appropriate uses within their policies and applicable requirements, preserving patient choice and access to a qualified human interpreter.

Language access is also a strategic performance driver for healthcare organizations, as effective communication influences patient understanding and experience, clinical outcomes, workforce efficiency and financial performance.

Equiti's customers include Wellstar Health System, Corewell Health, NYU Langone and Lee Health. Lexi works with a growing pipeline of federally qualified health centers and community providers including Lowell Community Health Center, which serves one of the most multilingual communities in Massachusetts.

As general-purpose AI gets better at translation, a healthcare-specific interpretation platform has distinct advantages, Huber asserted.

"Healthcare communication involves clinical meaning, cultural context, jargon and acronyms during situations where people may be frightened, vulnerable or unsure how to ask a question. Our job is to remove those communication barriers, and that requires understanding the care environment, fitting into clinical workflows and knowing when a qualified human interpreter needs to be involved," she said. "That is where Equiti’s experience matters. We bring the relationships, service infrastructure and human expertise developed through more than two decades of healthcare interpretation, alongside Lexi’s technology and team."

Huber said she envisions broader uses of Lexi's AI language support in healthcare workflows. "A patient’s need to communicate continues after the conversation with a clinician ends. Lexi already supports text-based messaging, including translation of text provided by a care team, and can even leave voicemail messages for patients. That creates opportunities to help patients access information and communicate between visits. Helping someone navigate follow-up care is a natural direction for that work, like understanding the next step, connecting with the right office or arranging an appointment. The value is in making it easier for patients to act on the care plan they have been given and ask for help along the way," she said.

"We built Lexi to fit the way healthcare teams actually work, bringing immediate language support into the devices and workflows they already use,” Siddharth UR, co-founder and chief product officer of Lexi, said in a statement. “As part of Equiti, we can extend that experience across the patient journey and connect it to a broader language access model built around the needs of each encounter.”

Lexi will operate alongside Martti under Equiti, with the teams working together on implementation and integration across healthcare workflows. Equiti will work with each customer to determine how the solutions fit within its language access program, clinical environment, and organizational policies.
