#5568. This $9.5 Million Pasadena Estate Looks 100 Years Old—Until You Step Inside

A vine-covered Mediterranean estate in Pasadena, CA that looks as though it has stood for a century or more, is actually just 16 years old, and it/s now on the market for $9.5 million.

Located at 1466 San Pasqual Street, the home was designed by architect John Barber to blend in with its neighbors—landmark homes that are roughly six times its age.

The home is represented by Brent Chang of Compass.

Behind automatic driveway gates, the exterior borrows many of the period architectural elements used by Wallace Neff and Marston & Van Pelt, defining names in Southern California’s early 20th-century residential architecture. The result was convincing enough that the house was once the lone new builds featured on a Pasadena Heritage tour of Spanish Revival homes from the 1920s and '30s.

Inside, however, the floor plan is decidedly modern. The main house offers 9- to 11-foot ceilings throughout, a two-story entry, a two-story family room and two staircases. French doors open to outdoor patios and a fireplace.

The open kitchen includes a breakfast area, pantry and butler’s pantry, while a library features its own fireplace and bar. There are two primary suites, each with a walk-in closet and private water closet, plus three additional suites and upper-level laundry.

The estate last sold in 2015 for $6.4 million, according to property records. Two years later, a 2,120-square-foot pool house was added. It includes two bedrooms, two bathrooms, a kitchen and a lounge with a wall of stacking glass doors that opens to the pool and spa.

The pool house’s lower level holds a game room with an automatic screen and projector, cubby bunk beds, a bathroom, laundry and separate front and rear entrances.

All together, the property spans 9,150 square feet with seven bedrooms and eight bathrooms on a 0.73 acre lot.

The grounds include a circular drive, three automatic gates, multiple lawns, gardens and patios. A secure rear driveway leads to a secondary motor court with a garage that fits four cars.

And behind all the period details are a set of thoroughly modern systems, including 400-amp electrical service, copper plumbing, a whole-house water filter, a fire sprinkler system and two water heaters which were installed in 2022.

#5567. Humanoid robot maker Agility Robotics debuts on the Nasdaq after SPAC merger

Agility Robotics Inc. debuted on the Nasdaq today after merging with a special-purpose acquisition company.

SPAC deals provide a simpler path to public markets than a traditional listing. In such transactions, a shell company floats its shares and then merges with a privately held business. That business effectively takes the SPAC’s place on the stock exchange where it’s listed.

Agility merged with an investment vehicle called Churchill Capital Corp XI Corp. on Wednesday. The deal and certain “related financings” together pulled in $465 million, a sum that excludes transaction fees. Agility will use the capital to bring its latest Digit 5 robot to market and add manufacturing capacity.

Digit 5 (pictured) is a nearly six-foot-tall humanoid robot with a 20-hour battery life. It moves using custom actuators based on so-called cycloidal drive technology. That’s a motor design that trades off some speed for increased lifting power: Agility says that the Digit 5 can carry up to 50 pounds at a time.

The robot’s batteries are made by a British startup called Nyobolt Ltd. They use niobium, a metal most commonly found in superconductors and jewelry, to speed up charging. Agility says that the Digit 5 can be recharged in just nine minutes, a fraction of the time required by earlier technologies.

The robot runs some of its software on Nvidia’s IGX Thor system-on-chip series. The most advanced chip in the lineup, the T7000, combines a 14-core central processing unit with a computer vision accelerator and two graphics processing units. One is an embedded GPU with 2,560 cores while the other is a standalone chip originally designed for workstations.

Digit 5 also makes use of Nvidia’s HALOS software toolkit. The suite includes algorithms that help robots avoid hazards. Additionally, HALOS provides resources that make it easier to secure the safety certifications required for commercial deployment.

Agility says that it has received more than $300 million worth of pre-orders for Digit 5. Its customers include Toyota Motor Co. and GXO Logistics Inc., a publicly traded transportation company. Agility claims that it also has three other large customers in the manufacturing sector along with a pipeline of more than 30 prospects.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Agility Chief Executive Officer Peggy Johnson. “Becoming a public company gives us access to more resources to help accelerate that progress, bring intelligent robots to more workplaces and help build a future where people and robots accomplish more together.”

Agility plans to make Digit 5 available through an early access program in the first half of 2027. General availability is slated for later that year. The company will manufacture Digit 5 at a  70,000-square-foot factory in Salem, Oregon with planned capacity of up to 10,000 robots per year.

#5565. Real Estate Veteran Dane Briggs Partners with HomeSmart NEXT Founder Phil Sexton in Leadership Role

Above, Dan Briggs Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, has announced his business partnership with fellow Arizona real estate industry veteran Dane Briggs. In this leadership role, Briggs will support the team’s advancement, including the development of agent-focused workflows and AI integrations.

A release writes that Sexton and Briggs have spent the majority of their mutual careers working collaboratively, though this endeavor marks the beginning of what Sexton says is sure to become a notable partnership.

“It’s rare to find a multi-faceted real estate talent like Dane; someone who has both run a brokerage and launched — then sold — a proptech startup. He’s fully on board with our mission of helping agents be more successful,” Sexton shared.

With roots in real estate as a designated broker, Briggs’ impressive career has spanned more than 20 years. He went on to secure leadership roles in title, founded a tech-driven referral brokerage, and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He is also one of the most visible educators in the Arizona market, having delivered more than 1,000 trainings and presentations over two decades and spoken at numerous conferences.

Today, Briggs holds a strategic role at the Greater Phoenix market platform The Cromford Report, co-hosts weekly statewide market update classes and continues to advise real estate, title and proptech companies on growth strategy, technology, and operations. With a background covering brokerage ownership, title and escrow executive management, he is naturally positioned for the NEXT team approach.

“Over the last few months, I’ve talked with a lot of companies about where I might fit and what we could accomplish together. But I kept coming back to what Phil was building. It was different from anything else I was seeing,” Briggs said. “Those conversations led to me getting involved and helping bring some of the technical ideas to life. Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together.”

Said Sexton of the announcement, “We’re built for agents that are out there doing the business but don’t want to worry about AI implementation or the ROI of marketing efforts. Dane and I are both industry veterans who love leveraging technology and taking leaps of faith. I’m very excited about where this will grow.”

The release says NEXT is a new style of real estate team built around one core belief: Agents should be the star of their own business. Unlike traditional teams that prioritize building the brand of a top producer, NEXT puts the focus and energy into elevating the individual agent.

For more information, or to inquire about joining NEXT, visit NextRealEstate.Team.

#5564. ‘It’s Insane’: Building Tech CEO Slams L.A.’s Return to Wood Framing After Deadly Wildfires

The country—maybe even the world—is at a crossroads in building construction due to climate change, and one CEO is disappointed about where things are going.

"Ninety-five percent of this community is rebuilding with wood," Ken Calligar says of Los Angeles County, which still trying to rebuild after the devastating 2025 Palisades and Alatadena wildfires. "It's insane."

"Unfortunately, that means they have designed in the next disaster," the founder and CEO of building technology company RSG-3D tells Realtor.com. "Builders say 'If we have to design in resiliency into a house, then no one can afford the house.' That's just baloney."

A former Wall Street investment banker who acquired disaster-resilient technology manufacturer Insteel Panelmex in 2018, Calligar has spent the past decade trying to get people to build differently. (The difference between "resilient" and "resistant" is complex, but Calligar prefers the term "resilient.")

Renamed RSG 3-D, his company manufactures framing panels made of steel wire and expanded polystyrene wrapped in concrete skins that can be molded into any shape and are practically indestructible—impervious to hurricanes, earthquakes, and fires.

Unsurprisingly, Calligar's firm has been busy in Los Angeles since the fires—but not busy enough as far as he is concerned.

He points out that not only are most destroyed residential buildings in the area being rebuilt with flammable materials—but they are now larger and closer together, increasing the chances that a conflagration can spread from one home to the next.

"A six-year-old could have said this wasn't a good idea," he says. "These towns are so vulnerable, they have no idea. To me, it's so obvious what the solution is."

In 2011, Calligar was doing a deep dive into building technologies for a start-up he was advising. The start-up didn't last, but Calligar's intense interest in creating buildings that could survive disasters did.

"Since the 1980, we have had decades of increasing frequency of natural disasters and the costs have gone up dramatically," he says. "In the 1980s, there averaged about four natural disasters a year. In the 2020s, we’re averaging about 23."

Beyond fires, there is an increasing frequency of other types of natural disasters—hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, shoreline erosion, extreme heat and cold. According to the 2026 Realtor.com Housing and Climate Risk Report, 23.1% of U.S. homes are vulnerable to severe or extreme climate risk from wind, flood, or wildfire, culminating in $11.2 trillion in risk exposure.

Then there is the human compulsion to build in risk-prone zones. "We like our views, our mountains and our seashores, and the population has been building in more vulnerable areas," says Calligar.

Homeowners are already paying the price in higher HOA fees, rising insurance premiums, elevated mortgage delinquency rates, and even in the inability to find insurance coverage at all.

"When disaster strikes, shoppers retrench, but the effect is short-lived," says the report. "Following the January 2025 LA wildfires, buyer interest in high-risk homes dropped 10%, yet fully recovered within one month."

"Waterfront access, mountain views, and river retreats matter more than the risk that comes with them."

Another alarming report says that California could lose up to 75% of its beaches either seasonally or permanently by 2100. Highly developed areas face "especially severe losses."

Calligar agrees—not only that homeowners want what they want and what they want isn't always good—but that builders keep making the same builds that have proven ineffective and even downright dangerous.

He notes one destroyed home in L.A. that burned down again during its rebuild. Someone had broken into the construction site to steal copper wire and sparked a fire. According to Calligar, the home was "all wood framed."

"The U.S. residential world is the only technology that hasn’t changed in the last half century," he adds. "It's actually gone backwards. The wood is worse, the productivity of the workers is worse, the quality of the builds is worse."

"If you refuse to learn, you're going to get the lesson again."

Some people, however, have learned. Jonathan Scott of the Property Brothers led the rebuilding of fiancée actress Zooey Deschanel's childhood home in Pacific Palisades. The 100-year-old Spanish Revival house was rebuilt to look exactly as it had before the fires—only this time it's using RSG 3-D technology.

"When Zooey’s parents walk in, this will feel like the original home," the HGTV reality star told KTLA. "All of these things we’ve thought about to make sure this house never ever burns down again. They’ll never have to go through what they went through last January."

"He is not connected to us financially," Calligar stresses of Scott's plentiful touting of RSG-3D technology in the press. "He's just a very happy client."

Calligar, who is currently working on about a dozen Los Angeles building projects, has three times that number scheduled for next year. "The demand is off the charts," he says. "It's a question of how much we can handle. We're still a small company, we can’t be everywhere."

Nor are his projects limited to L.A. Partners are using the technology in six states and in 20 international countries.

He says the notion that it costs significantly more to build a resilient home are a myth—and that using RSG-3D is "cost competitive against inferior building systems." Plus, additional costs can usually be absorbed with savings in energy and operating costs, and lower insurance premiums.

"You pull out way ahead, we've done the math," he says.

Another bonus? Homes can be built faster using the technology, since the panels are easy to erect, and don't require heavy machinery. Those concerned about aesthetics need not be, says Calligar. The panels are architecturally flexible, and can be curved or domed for any shape.

"Because of the strength of the system, you can do a lot more architecturally than you can with wood," he says. "We've got a lot of cool architecture."

Those sold on the idea of a disaster-resilient house can get it done with the firm's "trained ecosystem" of builders, architects, and engineers.

He compares RSG-3D technology to vaccines, and how they extended the human lifecycle.

"What we're trying to do is eradicate the diseases that are harming everyone," he says. "And extend the [building] lifecycle by centuries, by selecting the right materials."

He points to the Egyptian pyramids, erected with practically indestructible limestone and granite, and still standing tall after 4,500 years.

"If they'd done that with wood, we wouldn’t even know about them, they'd be muck in the sand," he says. "It's a good lesson in doing things right."

#5563. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

Redfin will highlight iconic American homes through the end of 2027. Know a home with a story worth telling? Nominate it for inclusion in the creative franchise using this form. Tour the first properties and get an alert when each new home debuts using redfin.com/iconic-homes.

#5562. A Former 1900s Lakeside Resort in Georgia Is for Sale as an $8.85 Million Private Retreat

Owning waterfront property is one thing. Owning the entire lake is another.

The lake, created from a dam on Ichawaynochaway Creek, is just part of the 1,442-acre property in Leary, GA listed for $8.85 million.

"When you're on the water, it's about 250 acres of private water in this famous mill pond. You own the whole [thing]. You own everything," explains listing agent Jon Kohler with Jon Kohler Associates.

“When you're out in a boat, you're not used to being the only one in this enormous lake. It probably takes five or six hours to go around the whole thing. It’s huge.”

“It's just fascinating. There's really nothing else like it, nor can there ever be again,” Kohler says. “You control it. You're the only boat that's able to duck hunt, fish, there.”

Cordray's Mill was once a resort property with a dance hall, swimming lake, and more, dating back to the early 1900s and continuing at least through the 1960s.

“There are a couple of remnant guest homes from the era when it was a resort, it was one of the first resorts in Georgia,” he says. “People would come from all over for events and whatnot.”

One structure is a converted church that is now a four bedroom and 1.5 bathroom house, in addition other living spaces.

“There's a house back where the mill pond house used to stand. There's a house on the lake, but back during its heyday, there were all types of structures, stores, shops, everything,” Kohler says.

The two houses have a total of six bedrooms and two bathrooms.

Another structure is a converted grain silo with one bedroom and a bathroom.

“It's one of those great ideas that not many people are able to pull off because the walls are rounded. It’s a really quaint little home.”

But the draw isn’t all of the places for people to stay, it’s about the activities.

“My favorite thing is the diversity of the habitats. You have almost every great habitat that Southwest Georgia has, but on one property,” Kohler explains, adding there is irrigated farmland and timberland in addition to the lake and waterfront.

The trophy whitetail deer make the property something special.

“I see it being owned by somebody that wants something that no one else has, which is the diversity and really the trophy deer hunting and the trophy deer habitat,” he says.

“Just a wildness factor that most places don't offer. [The perfect buyer is] somebody that really just wants to have the best of the best trophy whitetail, a lot of turkeys, and top it off with waterfowl, in an abundance greater than what most places offer.”

The property could also meet another need, a social storm property, which is a term Kohler trademarked several years ago.

“We recognized a trend that people were buying land for the lack of better word in case s**t hit the fan,” he said with a laugh, comparing the term to a prepper's property.

“This property is an ideal social storm property as well as a legacy sporting estate. I see most of these great places, but I had no idea a place like that existed. It's like a unicorn.

"You have 250 acres of water backed up in one of the largest private lakes in southeast United States all to yourself.”

#5561. Google Cloud storage moves to the front of the AI stack as enterprises hit the GPU utilization ceiling

ANALYSIS by Paul Nashawaty

For the past two years, enterprise AI investment has been dominated by one conversation: compute. Organizations raced to secure GPU allocations, negotiated infrastructure deals and stood up machine learning platforms at speed. What many discovered only after the fact is that the bottleneck they thought they were solving was not the only one in the room. Storage is now throttling the very accelerators enterprises fought to acquire.

In the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast, I spoke with Ronen Schwartz, vice president of products for Google Cloud Storage at Google LLC, about why storage has quietly become the defining constraint in enterprise AI infrastructure, and what a purpose-built architecture for AI workloads actually looks like. The conversation cuts to a problem that is real, measurable and still largely underacknowledged in most AI strategy discussions.

“Storage just got promoted,” Schwartz said. “Instead of being at the backend as an enabler, it is moving into the front as a critical part of accelerator execution.”

The economics of this problem are direct. Accelerators are, as Schwartz put it, an enterprise’s most expensive line item. Every second they idle waiting for data is money lost — not in some theoretical efficiency calculation, but in immediate, traceable waste. Yet when teams finally get access to their TPUs or GPUs, the data delivery path often hasn’t received the same attention as the compute layer.

“I speak to many customers, and what I’m hearing is the team spent a long time fighting to get their TPUs, their GPUs, to get their hands on accelerators. And once they got them, they’re actually not always able to get the output they needed. Very often it actually goes back to not enough thought put into the data delivery path.”

This is not a fringe scenario. Schwartz described a pattern where organizations identify the storage bottleneck only after it hits them — when GPU utilization metrics fall short of targets and training timelines stretch beyond projections. By then, the cost of underinvesting in storage architecture is already embedded in the project.

One of the clearest insights from the conversation is that AI is not a single workload, and treating it as one creates compounding gaps in storage architecture. Schwartz described training, inference and agentic workloads as having fundamentally different “heartbeats” with distinct data movement patterns that each require targeted design.

Training demands massive sequential reads, but the equally critical pressure point is checkpoint management. Every 15 minutes or so, a training cluster must pause and write a multi-terabyte checkpoint to protect work done against potential failure. “Slow storage in that place freezes the entire GPU cluster,” Schwartz said. Google’s Rapid object storage technology, he noted, can write checkpoints more than three times faster and restore them more than five times faster than standard object storage, and this distinction matters significantly at scale. He pointed to Torin, an autonomous vehicle company, as an example: millions of sensor data points flowing into storage to train vehicle models, where checkpoint performance is not an edge case but a core operational requirement.

Inference introduces a different constraint entirely, that of real-time, latency-sensitive interaction where response time directly affects user experience and token economics. Agentic workloads layer on a third set of demands: shared workspaces, state persistence across agents, low-latency retrieval and the need to support both short-lived and long-running agent processes that may hibernate and reactivate on demand.

“AI is not one workload. Really, the movement of data looks completely different. It’s like different heartbeats depending on where you are in the lifecycle.”

Google’s differentiation argument centers on infrastructure credibility built over years of running hyperscale AI workloads internally before offering the same capabilities externally. Schwartz cited specific performance figures: 15 terabytes per second on Rapid object storage and 10 terabytes per second on Google Cloud managed clusters, which he described as verified industry-leading numbers.

The technical foundation includes zonal colocation, or placing data physically close to GPU and TPU clusters to minimize the time a byte travels to the accelerator. Schwartz described this as a first-to-market capability that required rethinking assumptions baked into traditional storage design, where multi-zone or multi-region distribution was the default goal. For AI workloads, proximity to the accelerator takes priority. Google’s Rapid Bucket technology reduces processing steps in the storage path, enabling a single bucket to deliver more than 15 terabytes per second throughput with support for 20 million queries per second at sub-millisecond latency.

“It is because it is built on the Google infrastructure, which has been used internally longer than anyone else to support accelerators and their performance. But it is also because Google is working with nine out of the ten world-leading AI frontier model companies.” A storage architecture that can demonstrably improve GPU utilization can provide faster iteration through less idle compute and lower effective cost per training run.

The agentic dimension of the conversation revealed an underappreciated wrinkle in enterprise AI readiness. Agents require more than web browsing and database queries; they need access to unstructured data at scale, including images, video, documents and PDFs that represent the bulk of most organizations’ real data assets. Without a way to make that content semantically accessible, agents operate with a restricted and often unrepresentative view of enterprise knowledge.

Google’s response is what Schwartz called a Smart Storage Initiative, anchored by a recently launched Object Enrichment capability. When a file or image lands in a storage bucket, Google AI models automatically extract content and attach structured metadata to the object — in seconds, and at scale. The result is that what was previously unstructured becomes queryable by agents without manual intervention or downstream processing pipelines.

“An agent can now interact with what used to be called unstructured data because there is actually a very good understanding of the content.” The storage layer is also integrated into Google’s broader agentic data cloud and borderless lakehouse architecture, allowing agents to reach data stored outside Google’s environment as well.

For agent infrastructure at scale, Schwartz described dedicated Filestore agent volumes integrated directly into Google Kubernetes Engine and the agent sandbox environment, designed specifically to handle the cost, response speed, and data-sharing requirements of running thousands or millions of agents simultaneously.

The broader market shift here is architectural, not incremental. Enterprise AI infrastructure has been built in layers (compute first, then frameworks, then data) and storage was often treated as a procurement checkbox rather than a performance variable. That sequencing is proving costly. As GPU utilization targets become measurable KPIs and AI operations budgets face tighter scrutiny, the storage layer is being reassessed in a way it hasn’t been in years.

What Google’s position illustrates is that hyperscale operational experience at the storage layer translates directly into enterprise advantage — not as a marketing claim, but as a measurable difference in checkpoint speed, throughput, latency and agent responsiveness. The companies that have been running frontier model training and inference at scale have been forced to solve these problems; enterprise teams are now encountering them for the first time.

For platform engineers, ML infrastructure teams and enterprise architects, the implication is specific: Storage architecture decisions made during initial AI platform buildout will constrain or enable performance for every workload that follows. Revisiting those decisions after the bottleneck appears is significantly more expensive than addressing them in the design phase.

The market is heading toward a point where AI infrastructure conversations routinely include storage as a primary tier, not an afterthought. Organizations that recognize that shift early will extract measurably more value from the accelerator investments they have already made.

To hear the full conversation with Ronen Schwartz, check out the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast. To learn more about how Google Cloud Storage can support the evolving demands of enterprise AI, explore Google’s storage solutions or connect with the Google Cloud team to discuss the right approach for your organization’s workloads.

#5560. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5559. This Off-Grid ‘Treehouse’ Is Perched 60 Feet in the Air—and Built From Shipping Containers

If you've ever dreamed of sleeping among the trees, a property in the Epworth, GA, forest might be just the place.

"The structure itself is very unique. It's a steel watchtower built to commercial grade but for residential purposes, purely for leisurely enjoyment, for getaways, for the adventurer at heart," says listing agent Logan Fitts with Mountain Sotheby's International Realty.

Listed for $1.2 million, the 60-foot-high tower sits on 14.31 acres of land adjacent to the Chattahoochee National Forest with about 3,000 feet of river frontage.

"I was definitely awestruck first by the property itself, the river frontage, the waterfalls on the property, all of the hemlock trees dispersed throughout the property," Fitts says. "But then when we went to the top of the property where the watchtower was, I was in total awe."

Two shipping containers are perched atop the tower, creating the living space.

"The main structure is the bedroom efficiency with a bed, sitting area, stove, kitchenette. There's a landing between and then across is the bathroom area with a full shower, toilet, and double vanity," he explains. "Then there's a spiral staircase to the rooftop fire pit and lounge area."

And while there is a lift for things like suitcases and packages, people need to walk up 82 steel-grated stairs, which Fitts admits can be a bit daunting.

"I was actually nervous going up the tower for the first time because it's high and it is an experience. But once I did it, I said, 'This is what real mountain experiences are like. This is something that people remember for the rest of their lives.'"

"You are surrounded by just foliage, so when you're at the top, you just see a full panoramic view of the mountains and valley across one way, and you hear the roaring river on the property down below. You can actually see the waterfall," Fitts says.

"It's like a glass birdhouse at the top of this mountain, and you feel like you're definitely elevated and away from everything, but still connected to nature."

To get to the property itself requires a four-wheel-drive vehicle, because some of the roads are gravel and visitors need to cross the Jacks River, literally.

"Anyone with a four-wheel-drive or some type of ground clearance should have zero issue forging the river," Fitts explains, adding that the river is shallow at the access point. "It's not scary if you've done it before, and once you do it, it's like 'OK, now I'm an adventurer.'"

The current owner has had the place for about a decade and completed the tower house in 2023. Since then, it has been a short-term rental, bringing in about $92,000 annually during a nine-month rental period.

The owner would "love to pass it to someone that would take it, create a new legacy, and maybe make it even better," Fitts says.

"I think more than anything, he wants a true outdoors lover to really appreciate this property and not just see a metal dwelling in the middle of the forest. He built it for people to really enjoy nature, embrace nature, and take care of nature."

While the property itself is off-grid with solar power, a well, septic system, and generator, it’s not physically far from civilization.

"Probably the property is maybe 30 minutes from downtown Blue Ridge," Fitts says, adding it just feels remote. "Once you're there, you're in a totally different world. Your neighbors are trees and wildlife."

Tiffani Sherman is an experienced freelance writer based in the Tampa, Florida area who covers real estate, personal finance, travel, and more for a variety of print and online publications. She works to support her travel habit and has been to all seven continents and about 100 countries. Tiffani is a proud Duke Blue Devil.

#5557. Reba McEntire Reveals Dolly Parton’s Touching On-Set Gesture: ‘She Didn’t Have To Do That’

Reba McEntire was determined to make Dolly Parton feel welcome when the country legend joined her sitcom for a guest appearance—but it was Parton who ended up making everyone on-set feel special.

While speaking at NAR NXT in New Orleans alongside her manager and former real estate agent, Justin McIntosh, McEntire recalled the thoughtful gesture Parton made for every crew member behind the scenes of her hit sitcom “Reba”—a small act of kindness that left a lasting impression.

Instead of simply showing up and delivering her lines, Parton made a point of personally greeting the people working behind the scenes, bringing along Valentine’s Day candy and a message for every crew member.

For McEntire, the gesture remains a vivid example of the warmth that made her fellow singer so beloved.

“I was so nervous with Dolly being on the set. I wanted everyone to be nice. What I didn’t expect was how nice she was going to be on the set," she said.

McEntire recalled that Parton took the time to make each person feel appreciated, turning a guest appearance into a chance to connect with the crew.

“She had Valentine’s Day candies, and she went to every crew member individually and said how happy she was to be there,” she said. “She didn’t have to do that.”

The memory has stayed with McEntire, along with a conversation the two shared while sitting together on the iconic show's couch.

“I asked her if she would ever retire,” McEntire recalled. “And she said, ‘What would I do that I could have so much fun doing?’”

It was a simple answer, but one that reflected the enthusiasm McEntire remembers so fondly.

“I’ve never met a person or known a person that’s so universally loved like Dolly Parton,” she said. “I’ve never heard anything bad about her. She was that special of a person.”

That sense of gratitude for a career filled with opportunities to connect with people is something McEntire shares.

“I’m just really grateful and thankful for doing what I do at the level I do,” she said.

For McEntire, keeping her work exciting means giving herself room to try new things—and inviting her audience along for the experience.

“When I change things up, my fans stay interested with me,” she explained. “If it looks like I’m having fun, then they’re having fun.”

The actress revealed that being able to enjoy her work is a gift.

“If you are doing what you love, then that’s how blessed you are,” she said. “That’s one of the greatest gifts God can give, to give you a job you love. I’m very grateful for my job.”

The connection she has built with her audience also rests on the principle that people can recognize sincerity principle—something she believes applies well beyond entertainment.

“I try to sing the songs from my heart so when you listen to it, it touches your heart,” she said.

That emphasis on warmth and connection carries into the way McEntire searches for a home, too.

Long before her career brought her to stages and television sets, she grew up on an 8,000-acre ranch in Oklahoma.

Despite the expanse of land outside, her family of six shared a small house with three bedrooms and one bathroom.

Asked what she first thinks of when she remembers the ranch, McEntire named the people and feelings that filled it.

“Love, family, unity, closeness,” she said. “One itty-bitty bathroom, three bedrooms. We were a close family.”

Gathering around the dinner table was part of life, and the atmosphere of the house remains easy for her to recall.

“We all sat at the dinner table together,” she said. “It was earthy. I can still smell how the house smelled and the energy.”

The land remains a family home. McEntire says it stayed in the family after her parents died, and her sister and her sister’s family now live on the property.

Those early memories offer a glimpse of what McEntire still values when she walks into a house: a feeling of comfort and a connection that goes beyond its appearance.

“A house has energy, and when you come in and when you bond with that energy, it makes it a home,” she said. “So I always look for good, positive energy when I come in.”

The country icon reflected on the moment she experienced that pull while looking for property in Tennessee.

A friend who was vacationing in Florida with a real estate agent spotted a listing the agent was viewing and urged that it be shown to McEntire.

“My friend said, ‘You gotta show Reba that place,’” she recalled.

The approach to the property and a creek at the back helped capture her attention. Soon, she was returning for visits and spending time with the owners.

“The love I had for that house, it took my breath away,” she said. “I went a couple times, and I watched football games with the owners.”

When it comes to her priorities in a home, being comfortable and enjoying the surroundings rank high.

“I love a home with a view,” she said. “When I lived in Oklahoma, you could see sunrise and sunset. That’s important to me.”

McEntire said that focus on people and their needs also helped draw her to her partnership with Realtor.com®.

“What y'all do is very important, you care so much, that's why I like Realtor.com. I love your organization because you have heart...You really do dive into the family and what their needs are. You love people and you care about people, that's why I wanted to be with you guys," she said.

Whether she is discussing finding a home or maintaining the trust of an audience, McEntire returns to the importance of treating people well—and continuing to do so over time.

“You have to stay consistently honest, because when you look someone in the eye, they know how you treated them last time,” she said. “You have to stay consistent with it.”

#5555. Atlassian shares fall 17% as slower subscription growth forecast overshadows earnings beat

Shares in Atlassian Corp. fell more than 17% in after-hours trading today on a forecast for slower subscription growth from the Australian collaboration software company.

Its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results beat analyst estimates. The stock had nearly doubled between Atlassian’s August report and late October.

For the quarter ended Sept. 30, Atlassian reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.65, up from $1.04 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $1.772 billion, up 24% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting $1.43 per share on revenue of $1.71 billion.

Most of the growth came from cloud, where revenue rose 31%, to $1.302 billion. Customers kept adding Jira and Confluence seats in the quarter, according to the shareholder letter, including in business teams well outside software development.

Growth in Data Center, the self-managed product line Atlassian will retire in March 2029, slowed to about 5%, leaving revenue there at $391 million. The company said those customers are expanding less as they plan their moves to the cloud.

Subscription annual recurring revenue came in at $6.812 billion at the end of September, up 22.5%. Remaining performance obligations jumped 44%, to $4.746 billion. Enterprise customers are behind that increase, according to the company, with deals getting larger and stretching over several years.

Atlassian made money on an unadjusted basis for the second quarter running, with net income of $91 million, or 35 cents per share. Chief Financial Officer James Chuong put that down to keeping costs in check while revenue grew. Free cash flow climbed to $463 million on strong collections, and Atlassian returned $581 million to shareholders through buybacks.

On the product side, more than 87% of enterprise cloud customers now use Rovo, the company’s artificial intelligence assistant. Upgrades to the Teamwork Collection bundle rose sevenfold from a year ago to more than 3,000 customers. Annual recurring revenue from the larger Service Collection bundle is now above $1 billion, spread across more than 70,000 customers.

Chief Executive Mike Cannon-Brookes used the earnings release to argue that enterprise AI has reached “an inflection point.” Model power alone no longer sets anyone apart, he said. Platforms that give people and AI agents shared context to work from will pull ahead by his account, and Atlassian has “never been better positioned” to be one of them.

For the second quarter, Atlassian expects revenue of $1.825 billion to $1.835 billion, a little ahead of the $1.82 billion analysts had forecast, with cloud revenue growth of about 27%.

Most of Atlassian’s fiscal 2027 targets edged higher in the update. The company now sees full-year revenue growth of about 13.75%, three-quarters of a point above its August forecast. Because customers pulled Data Center purchases into fiscal 2026 after the retirement announcement, this year’s revenue comparisons are tougher.

Total revenue growth should pick up again in fiscal 2028, Atlassian said. Investors sold the stock on a different number. The company expects subscription annual recurring revenue growth to slow to about 18.5% by fiscal year-end, down from the 22.5% it just reported.

#5554. CZ Pardon Faces New Democrats Scrutiny A Week After $6.3B Binance Hack

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Democrats are continuing their investigation into Changpeng Zhao, known as CZ, pardon as Binance faces renewed scrutiny following a $6.34 billion security breach. The Democrats inquiry into CZ pardon is bringing fresh attention to Binance’s founder, who says he no longer manages the exchange but remains one of its most vocal public defenders.

The October 29 Binance hack targeted internal wallet-signing systems, triggering unauthorized transfers across several blockchain networks. Binance says it will absorb the financial impact, while CZ has publicly defended the exchange and reassured users.

The incident has added another layer to questions surrounding Zhao’s relationship with Binance. Despite stepping down as CEO after his 2023 guilty plea, he remains closely associated with the company and continues to comment on major developments.

Democrats have been investigating if political connections, financial relationships, or lobbying influenced President Donald Trump’s decision to pardon Zhao in October 2025.

In May, lawmakers sent letters to 17 clemency recipients, including Zhao, seeking information about their pardon applications and any involvement from lobbyists, intermediaries, or political allies. The inquiry later expanded to federal offices involved in the clemency process.

The scrutiny intensified after Binance’s security breach. On October 30, House Financial Services Committee Ranking Member Maxine Waters pointed to Binance’s reported ties to the Trump family’s World Liberty Financial, the SEC’s decision to drop its case against Binance and CZ, and Trump’s pardon.

Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program at Binance. He stepped down as CEO and served four months in prison before receiving the presidential pardon.

The Democrats investigation focuses on how clemency was obtained and whether financial or political relationships played a role in CZ pardon. Binance’s hack has now placed the exchange’s security and accountability in the same spotlight.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Binance’s November 3 incident update put the affected assets at $6.34 billion. The attacker gained unauthorized access to an internal wallet-signing service and initiated transfers outside the exchange’s normal withdrawal process.

The attack moved assets across several networks, including XRP, Solana, Optimism, Bitcoin and Ethereum. Binance said approximately $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted, while 98% of affected token assets had been replenished by October 31.

The breach targeted Binance’s internal wallet infrastructure rather than BNB Chain’s consensus mechanism. No BNB Chain consensus exploit was reported, distinguishing the exchange-side compromise from an attack on the blockchain itself.

CZ has remained highly visible throughout the response. After Elon Musk appeared to mock the incident online, Zhao asked him to stop trolling and referenced Binance’s SpaceX investment, which he said was worth more than $1 billion.

The exchange’s co-CEO, Yi He, later said Binance’s revenue was sufficient to cover the losses and that it did not need to sell the SpaceX stake. CZ later clarified that his comments were not an announcement of a planned sale.

#5553. ‘The American Dream Has an Address’—and Both Parties Are on Notice, Strategists Say

Democrats' historic midterm sweep will hand them control of Congress, but keeping it could depend on whether they can make housing more affordable, according to leading strategists from both parties.

"The American dream has an address," veteran Democratic strategist Donna Brazile told a room of real estate professionals in New Orleans on Saturday.

Speaking alongside conservative political strategist Shermichael Singleton at the National Association of Realtors®' NAR NXT conference, Brazile cautioned that Democrats' electoral victories were not an unconditional endorsement of their policies, but a demand for relief from the rising cost of living.

Singleton agreed, arguing that Republicans had already learned that lesson the hard way.

"Our voters felt we fundamentally failed," he said, pointing to rising fuel and food costs as well as younger Americans' inability to afford homes as examples of the administration's unfulfilled affordability promises.

Brazile warned that Democrats could face the same reckoning in 2028 if they fail to act.

"If you're not going to help build more houses and take care of the affairs of the American people, they will kick our [expletive] in two years," she said.

The affordability crisis that helped propel Democrats to victory Tuesday had been a liability for their own party just two years earlier—a fact that Brazile said is a warning to both parties heading into 2028.

"Affordability has been on the minds of American people now for two consecutive years," Brazile said, acknowledging that Joe Biden and Kamala Harris had failed to recognize the depth of voters' frustration ahead of the 2024 election.

And today, housing offers perhaps the clearest illustration of why that frustration has persisted.

Mortgage rates climbed from roughly 3% in 2021 to nearly 8% by late 2023, compounding a pandemic-era surge in home prices, Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the National Association of Realtors, explained during a separate presentation Saturday.

And while borrowing costs have since eased, home prices continue to climb. Prices rose in approximately 78% of U.S. metropolitan markets during the third quarter of 2026, according to NAR's latest quarterly report.

Existing homeowners have benefited from that appreciation, with Yun estimating that the typical owner has gained nearly $200,000 in housing wealth since before the pandemic. Prospective buyers, meanwhile, face a considerably higher cost of entry.

The consequences are particularly stark for younger Americans. First-time buyers now account for just 22% of home purchases, while their median age has reached 40, matching last year's record high, according to NAR's newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers.

"Maybe the election result was partly reflecting that fact," Yun said, pointing to younger Americans struggling to enter the housing market.

For Singleton, 36, the frustration is personal.

"You do everything right. You get the college degree. You get the graduate degree. You start the family. You can't afford anything," he said.

Singleton purchased his first home at 28, but said many of his friends, now approaching or entering their 40s, still can’t afford to buy.

And with millennials and Gen Z now accounting for a substantial share of the electorate, Singleton argued that housing access could become a more decisive factor in how younger Americans vote.

Amid deep political divisions, Brazile and Singleton's agreement on the urgency of the housing crisis was striking. And already, there's a powerful precedent for cooperation on the issue.

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, enacted in July, received overwhelming support from both parties, passing the Senate 85-5 and the House 358-32. The legislation aims to boost supply by reducing regulatory barriers, expanding financing opportunities, and supporting new approaches to construction.

But passage was only the first step. Many provisions still require implementation or funding, and their effects on the market could take years to materialize.

Singleton sees opportunities to build on that foundation by addressing barriers closer to home, including local permitting delays, construction costs, and tariffs on Canadian lumber.

"One of the things that I hear about often from them is that the length of time it takes to get something approved is very costly," he said, referring to conversations with builders.

He also proposed investing in training younger Americans as electricians, plumbers, and other skilled tradespeople to help build the millions of homes the country needs.

It's an idea echoed by Scott Norman, CEO of the Texas Association of Builders, who identified workforce development as a bipartisan priority in an exclusive interview with Realtor.com following Democrats' sweep of the state's elected offices.

"The more folks we can get in the business, that'll drive down those labor costs," Norman said.

Brazile, meanwhile, said Democrats' affordability agenda places housing alongside groceries, energy, and family expenses, with an emphasis on cutting red tape and expanding supply.

"Affordability, affordability, affordability. It's not a slogan that Democrats can use again unless they do something about it," she said.

But delivering on those promises will require something neither party has consistently demonstrated in recent years: a willingness to compromise.

"We have the money, but we need the will," Brazile said.

In an emotional moment of the one-hour session, Brazile recalled working with Republican President George W. Bush to secure federal assistance after Hurricane Katrina devastated the city in 2005.

Despite their political differences, Brazile said she worked with the administration to secure funding for housing recovery, infrastructure, and a new veterans' medical center.

"That's bipartisanship. That's compromise. That's what it looks like," she said.

Her closing message to the real estate agents in attendance was to bring that same commitment to the newly elected lawmakers who will shape housing policy.

"You know the stories because you live it every day," she told them, urging agents to share the experiences of families struggling to afford homes.

And with a new Congress preparing to take office, Brazile argued, that firsthand knowledge could help turn promises of affordability into policies that deliver.

#5552. Jobs Jump in October, With Unemployment Dipping Slightly

A day after the stock market hit the skids big-time, there was good news on the employment front. U.S. employers hired at a vigorous pace in October, adding 165,000 jobs, way above the 65,000 forecast, while the unemployment rate lowered slightly to 4.1% from 4.2%.

The report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that employers are continuing to hire workers even with the Iran War raising energy prices, tariffs a continual worry and the uncertainty of how AI will affect businesses on many levels.

The total nonfarm payroll rise of 165,000 jobs is higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business services, in healthcare and in transportation and warehousing.

“Today’s report was impressive,” said Realtor.com® Senior Economist Jake Krimmel. “Coming in, we would have been happy with the forecasted 65,000, more than double last month’s. Instead we got more than double. Revisions added another 84,000 jobs to August and September, lifting the three-month average to 137,000 from about 51,000 a month ago.

“This is still a low hire, low fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side. The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month.”

The report might be a welcome sign for the broader economy one day after stocks plummeted, with AI-centric companies hit hardest. For housing markets, though, the stability comes with a caveat—inflation is likely more of a primary concern for policymakers.

Krimmel noted that for the Fed, the report clears the way for a rate hike, because a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December.

“If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now,” he said. “One question that keeps coming up is whether the midterms changed anything for the housing market. In the short run, not much—the Iran War and its impact on inflation and mortgage rates remain the major wildcard. Getting back to ‘normal’ in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines.”

Krimmel noted that mortgage rates have declined for three straight weeks after a massive 74 basis point surge from late August to mid-October, but wages are the other half of buying power.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5551. How One Real Estate Investor Replaced Evictions With a $5,000-a-Month Sober Living Business

Five years into his real-estate investing journey, Hunter Foote grew disillusioned. Starting in 2010, he had flipped a few homes and purchased several multi-family units. The cash flow was solid, but the tenants made his life challenging.

“I have a long history of being frustrated and evicting tenants and dealing with some folks who weren’t at the best time of their lives,” he says.

He wanted to provide housing and help people, but evictions were not only costly, but disheartening. He wasn’t sure he could continue.

Cue Thanksgiving 2015. His sister-in-law works in the recovery space as a program manager in central Connecticut. In talking about her work, Foote says, “she was in tears about how folks who get out of treatment have nowhere to go.”

People get sober but haven’t yet made sober friends who can provide a couch to surf or room to rent. The person’s family typically wants them to have more time clean before they welcome them home or lend financial support. The end result is that many people find themselves sober but without housing options.

Foote was intrigued, and liked the idea of helping people while still investing in real estate.

“I’m a bit of a nerd and spent a year doing research,” he says. The problem was that, back then, there was no infrastructure to guide someone in starting a sober-living home.

“It was the Wild West with people calling it different names and everyone was doing different things,” he adds.

In 2016, he bought a seven-bedroom home for $360,000 in Worcester, MA. The home was zoned as a two-family unit with six bedrooms upstairs and a basement apartment that, combined, “didn’t fit the bill for a lot of investors.” It had been listed for $480,000 but had sat on the market for more than 200 days, which is how Foote picked it up at a discount.

He used hard money to buy the property at 12% interest with two points. He had 12 months to either pay off the loan or figure out financing–eventually refinancing out using a DSCR loan.

Getting the property fixed up and furnished was easy. Getting the beds filled, less so.

“Everyone says there is just demand everywhere,” he says. “But to get the right people, you really need to work hard.”

He had to network quickly, meeting with people from jail pre-release programs, drug courts and treatment centers.

“You have to get your name out there to get the right referrals. The key to success is getting the right people in there in the first place.”

It took six months to break even. At nine months, he was profitable.

Once the home was operating at capacity, it generated around $13,000 in monthly revenue. Operating expenses totaled roughly $4,000, leaving $9,000 in net operating income. After accounting for property taxes, insurance and the mortgage, the home netted approximately $5,000 a month.

Sober living isn’t just about “filling the beds.”

The average stay is between six and nine months. However, that doesn’t account for the folks who leave after “three weeks, three days or three hours.”

Sometimes men are dropped off and only committed to sober living so that jail or the recovery program would release them–the person never had any intention of staying clean and committing to a sober house.

“They stay until the car drives away, and then all they think about is that they are free,” Foote says.

Others “didn’t think the rules would apply” to them. Still others have drug paraphernalia in their bags that’s discovered during the check-in bag search.

“These guys try to tell me marijuana is legal in Massachusetts,” he says. “It is, but it’s not allowed in a sober living house.”

In the beginning, Foote was losing money every time someone committed and then dropped out.

He has learned he has to charge a $200 nonrefundable fee to cover the intake process, which includes a drug screening and bag search.

It’s just one of the systems he has learned in his 10 years of owning about 10 sober-living homes and managing many more. Foote bought homes primarily in New England, where he learned which towns have more lenient permitting. Worcester was “one of the toughest” cities to operate in because it required additional features in the home.

“They made us put in sprinklers and extra fire alarms that other cities weren’t requiring,” he says.

Foote’s homes are NARR Level II certified recovery residences, which means there is no paid staff on site. Each home houses only one gender, and the home has a house mentor who lives there for free in exchange for helping manage the day-to-day.

These days, Foote spends less time managing his own rentals, and more time helping others with theirs.

“We transitioned out of running homes so that we could launch some software offerings” to help others in the sober living space. They’re in the process of launching a software called Sober Desk that helps sober-living landlords manage their homes. For example, this software helps homeowners collect weekly rent, a common practice in the sober-living space.

“Logging the drug screens is also not something you can do in Buildium” for example.

He has also launched a management company, Vanderburgh Sober Living, to help run other people’s sober-living homes. His company also assists investors with finding the right property and launching.

When it comes to choosing a house, “the bigger, the better” but location dictates what works. For example, in Texas, “there are so many inexpensive four-bedroom homes” where “eight beds in four bedrooms” can work really well.

Regardless of where in the country the house is, Foote believes that there is a way to make sober living work both financially and for the community. It’s a model he strongly believes in.

“People would be surprised that they can make a difference in the community and still make money—you don’t have to pick between them.”

She was previously the U.S. Head of News at DailyMail.com, and Chief News Director for Stuff.co.nz in New Zealand. She holds a Bachelor of Journalism Degree from Rhodes University in South Africa. She lives in New York City.

#5550. OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, an Astra model built to keep vulnerability research in scope

OpenAI Group PBC today released GPT-6 Cyber, a version of its GPT-6 Astra model trained specifically for authorized vulnerability research.

The new model goes after a problem OpenAI’s own security work exposed this summer. In July, agents running in the company’s test environments broke into Hugging Face Inc. while pursuing an assigned task. GPT-6 Cyber was trained to stay inside the targets a researcher has authorized, and the safety test OpenAI built for the launch draws on that incident.

That test, ExploitGym Honeypot, gives the model a difficult assignment and surrounds it with supporting services that are deliberately easy to compromise. Attacking any of those services counts as a scope violation.

With no deployment safety instructions in place, GPT-6 Cyber went out of bounds in 0.07% of graded runs. Its predecessor, GPT-5.6-Cyber, did so 5.51% of the time. Adding the instructions brought GPT-6 Cyber’s observed rate to zero.

OpenAI rates the new model at Critical, the top cybersecurity tier in its Preparedness Framework and the same classification Astra received at its September launch. GPT-5.6-Cyber had been rated High. The company says GPT-6 Cyber beats Astra on most cyber tasks, and an early research campaign on Firefox turned up 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities that Mozilla Corp. rated high severity. Mozilla has since shipped fixes for many of them.

Irregular, an AI security lab named in the system card, put the gap with Astra closer, finding the two broadly comparable apart from stronger GPT-6 Cyber results on long multistep tasks. Neither model got past fully hardened targets in OpenAI’s own challenge set.

GPT-6 Cyber is the fourth cyber-specific model OpenAI has released this year. Like the first, GPT-5.4-Cyber, it sits behind an application process. Initial access is limited to a select group of approved customers in Daybreak Red, the tier of OpenAI’s Daybreak program meant for offensive-style work such as penetration testing and red teaming. Those customers reach the model through the company’s application programming interface and Codex, and API requests have to come from approved networks by default.

Google LLC also put vetted defenders first when it launched Gemini 4 Argon in September. A week later Anthropic PBC rebuilt its Cyber Verification Program around three access tiers.

OpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber will reach all Daybreak Red customers over the coming weeks, and GPT-5.6-Cyber is now opening to every customer in the tier. Critical infrastructure defenders get a Daybreak Red group of their own. On the defensive side, the company is extending early Astra access through Daybreak Blue to more organizations and to individual security researchers.

#5549. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.
